title: Chapter 133 — The Chase—First Day
paragraphs: That night, during the middle watch, when the old man — as he did from time to time — stepped out of the scuttle where he had been leaning and went to his pivot-hole, he suddenly thrust his face out fiercely and sniffed the sea air, the way a clever ship's dog will when the ship draws near some savage island. He declared that a whale must be close. Soon the whole watch could smell that peculiar odor which the living sperm whale sometimes gives off to a great distance; and no sailor was surprised when Ahab, after checking the compass, then the dog-vane, and then fixing the exact bearing of the smell as nearly as he could, quickly ordered the ship's course altered slightly and the sail shortened.

The shrewd thinking behind these movements was sufficiently proved at daybreak by the sight of a long slick on the sea directly and lengthwise ahead, smooth as oil, and resembling, in the pleated watery wrinkles bordering it, the polished metallic marks of some swift tidal rip at the mouth of a deep, rapid stream.
"Man the mastheads! Call all hands!"

Thundering on the forecastle deck with the butts of three clubbed handspikes, Daggoo woke the sleepers with such Judgment-Day claps that they seemed to be breathed out of the scuttle, so instantly did they appear, clothes in hand.
"What do you see?" cried Ahab, flattening his face to the sky.
"Nothing, nothing, sir!" was the sound hailing down in reply.
"Topgallant sails! Stunsails! Aloft and alow, and on both sides!"

All sail being set, he now cast loose the life-line, reserved for swaying him up to the main royal-masthead; and in a few moments they were hoisting him there. He was only two-thirds of the way aloft, peering ahead through the horizontal vacancy between the main-topsail and topgallant-sail, when he raised a gull-like cry in the air. "There she blows! — there she blows! A hump like a snow-hill! It is Moby Dick!"

Fired by the cry, which the three lookouts seemed to take up at the same moment, the men on deck rushed into the rigging to see the famous whale they had been pursuing so long. Ahab had now reached his final perch, some feet above the other lookouts, with Tashtego standing just below him on the cap of the topgallant-mast, so that the Indian's head was almost level with Ahab's heel. From this height the whale could now be seen a mile or so ahead, showing his high, sparkling hump at every roll of the sea and regularly jetting his silent spout into the air. To the credulous sailors it seemed the same silent spout they had seen so long ago in the moonlit Atlantic and Indian Oceans.
"And did none of you see it before?" cried Ahab, hailing the perched men all around him.
"I saw him almost that same instant, sir, that Captain Ahab did, and I cried out," said Tashtego.

"Not the same instant; not the same — no, the doubloon is mine; Fate kept the doubloon for me. Only I; none of you could have raised the White Whale first. There she blows! — there she blows! — there she blows! There again! — there again!" he cried, in long-drawn, lingering, measured tones, keeping time with the gradual lengthening of the whale's visible jets. "He's going to sound! In stunsails! Down topgallant-sails! Stand by three boats. Mr. Starbuck, remember, stay on board and keep the ship. Helm there! Luff, luff a point! So; steady, man, steady! There go flukes! No, no; only black water! All ready the boats there? Stand by, stand by! Lower me, Mr. Starbuck; lower, lower — quick, quicker!" And he slid through the air to the deck.
"He is heading straight to leeward, sir," cried Stubb, "right away from us; cannot have seen the ship yet."
"Be quiet, man! Stand by the braces! Hard down the helm! — brace up! Shiver her! — shiver her! So; well that! Boats, boats!"

Soon all the boats except Starbuck's were lowered; all the boat-sails were set and all the paddles working, and they shot to leeward with rippling speed, Ahab leading the charge. A pale, deathly glimmer lit up Fedallah's sunken eyes; a hideous movement gnawed at his mouth.

Like noiseless nautilus shells, their light prows sped through the sea; but they closed on the foe only slowly. As they came nearer, the ocean grew smoother still; it seemed to be drawing a carpet over its waves; it seemed a noon meadow, so serenely did it spread. At length the breathless hunter came so close to his seemingly unsuspecting prey that the whale's entire dazzling hump was plainly visible, sliding along the sea as if it were a thing apart, and ringed all the while by a revolving circle of the finest, fleecy, greenish foam. Beyond it he saw the vast, intricate wrinkles of the slightly projecting head. Ahead of the whale, far out on the soft waters patterned like a Turkish rug, went the glistening white shadow of his broad, milky forehead, with a musical rippling playfully keeping the shadow company; behind, the blue waters flowed in turn into the moving valley of his steady wake; and on either side bright bubbles rose and danced along beside him. But these were broken again by the light toes of hundreds of gay sea-birds softly feathering the sea between their fitful flights; and like some flagstaff rising from the painted hull of an argosy, the tall but shattered pole of a recent lance stuck up from the white whale's back; and every so often one of the cloud of soft-toed birds, hovering and skimming to and fro like a canopy over the fish, would silently perch and rock on this pole, its long tail feathers streaming like pennons.

A gentle joyousness — a mighty mildness of repose in swiftness — clothed the gliding whale. Not the white bull Jupiter, swimming away with the ravished Europa clinging to his graceful horns, his lovely, leering eyes turned sideways on the girl, rippling with smooth, bewitching speed straight for the bridal bower in Crete — not Jove, not that great majesty Supreme! — surpassed the glorified White Whale as he swam so divinely.

On each soft side — in step with the parted swell that, once it left him, flowed so far and wide away — on each bright side, the whale gave off enticements. No wonder there had been some among the hunters who, carried away and allured beyond words by all this serenity, had ventured to attack it, only to find, fatally, that this quietude was nothing but the garment of tornadoes. Yet calm, enticing calm, oh whale! You glide on before all who see you for the first time, no matter how many in that same way you may have tricked and destroyed before.

And so, through the calm serenity of the tropical sea, among waves whose hand-clapping was held back by overwhelming rapture, Moby Dick moved on, still keeping the full terrors of his submerged trunk out of sight and completely hiding the twisted hideousness of his jaw. But soon the front of him slowly rose out of the water; for an instant his whole marble-like body formed a high arch, like Virginia's Natural Bridge; and, waving his bannered flukes in the air in warning, the grand god revealed himself, sounded, and disappeared. Hovering, pausing and dipping on the wing, the white seabirds lingered longingly over the churning pool he left behind.
With oars peaked, blades raised clear of the water, and paddles down, the sheets of their sails adrift, the three boats now silently floated, awaiting Moby Dick's reappearance.

"An hour," said Ahab, standing rooted in the stern of his boat; and he gazed past the place where the whale had been, toward the dim blue spaces and wide, wooing emptiness to leeward. It lasted only an instant; for his eyes again seemed to whirl around in his head as he swept the circle of water. The breeze was freshening now; the sea began to swell.
"The birds! — the birds!" cried Tashtego.

In long Indian file, like herons taking wing, the white birds were now all flying toward Ahab's boat; and when they were within a few yards they began fluttering over the water there, wheeling round and round with joyous, expectant cries. Their vision was keener than man's; Ahab could find no sign in the sea. But suddenly, as he peered down and down into its depths, far down he saw a white living spot no bigger than a white weasel rising with wonderful speed and growing larger as it rose, until it turned, and then two long crooked rows of white, glistening teeth were plainly revealed, floating up from the unfathomable bottom. It was Moby Dick's open mouth and scrolled jaw, his vast, shadowed bulk still half blending with the blue of the sea. The glittering mouth yawned beneath the boat like a marble tomb with its door open; and with one sidelong sweep of his steering oar, Ahab whirled the boat aside from this tremendous apparition. Then, calling on Fedallah to change places with him, he went forward to the bow, seized Perth's harpoon, and ordered his crew to grip their oars and stand ready to back the boat astern.

Now, because the boat had been spun round on its axis in time, its bow was made to face the whale's head in advance, while the head was still under water. But as if he saw through this stratagem, Moby Dick, with that malicious intelligence ascribed to him, shifted himself sideways in an instant, as it were, shooting his pleated head lengthwise beneath the boat.

Through and through — through every plank and every rib — a thrill ran for an instant, as the whale, lying obliquely on his back in the manner of a biting shark, slowly and sensitively took the bows fully into his mouth, so that the long, narrow, scrolled lower jaw curled high up into the open air, and one of the teeth caught in a rowlock. The bluish pearl-white of the inside of the jaw was within six inches of Ahab's head, and reached higher than that. In this position the White Whale now shook the slight cedar boat as a mildly cruel cat shakes her mouse. Fedallah gazed with unastonished eyes and crossed his arms; but the tiger-yellow crew were tumbling over each other's heads to reach the farthest end of the stern.

And now the two springy gunwales were bending in and out as the whale toyed with the doomed boat in this devilish way; his body was submerged beneath the boat, so he could not be darted at from the bow, for the bow was almost inside him, as it were; and the other boats had involuntarily paused, as before a sudden crisis impossible to withstand. It was then that the monomaniac Ahab, furious at being so tantalizingly close to his foe — a closeness that put him, fully alive and helpless, in the very jaws he hated — frenzied by all this, seized the long bone with his bare hands and wildly strove to wrench it loose from its grip. As he strove in vain, the jaw slipped from him; the frail gunwales bent in, collapsed, and snapped, as both jaws, like enormous shears, slid further aft, bit the boat completely in two, and locked themselves shut again in the sea, midway between the two floating wrecks. These drifted apart, their broken ends drooping, the crew at the stern-wreck clinging to the gunwales and struggling to hold on to the oars in order to lash them across.

At that opening moment, before the boat was snapped, Ahab had been the first to see the whale's intent, from the crafty lifting of his head — a movement that loosened his hold for the time — and at that moment his hand made one final effort to push the boat out of the bite. But the boat, only slipping further into the whale's mouth and tilting sideways as it slipped, had shaken off his hold on the jaw and spilled him out as he leaned into the push; and so he fell flat on his face upon the sea.

Rippling away from his prey, Moby Dick now lay a little distance off, thrusting his oblong white head vertically up and down in the billows while slowly revolving his whole spindle-shaped body; so that whenever his vast wrinkled forehead rose — some twenty feet or more out of the water — the swells, now rising, broke dazzlingly against it with all their merging waves, vindictively tossing their shattered spray still higher into the air.* So, in a gale, the Channel billows, only half baffled, recoil from the base of the Eddystone lighthouse only to leap triumphantly over its summit with their scud.

*This motion is peculiar to the sperm whale. It gets its name (pitchpoling) because it is likened to the preliminary up-and-down poise of the whale-lance in the exercise called pitchpoling, described earlier. By this motion the whale must best and most comprehensively view whatever objects may be encircling him.

But soon, returning to a horizontal position, Moby Dick swam swiftly round and round the wrecked crew, churning the water sideways in his vengeful wake, as if whipping himself up to yet another and deadlier attack. The sight of the splintered boat seemed to madden him, as the blood of grapes and mulberries, cast before Antiochus's elephants in the book of Maccabees, maddened them. Meanwhile Ahab was half smothered in the foam of the whale's insolent tail, and too much of a cripple to swim — though he could still keep afloat, even in the heart of a whirlpool like that — and helpless Ahab's head could be seen like a tossed bubble that the slightest chance shock might burst. From the broken-off stern of the boat Fedallah watched him with mild indifference; the clinging crew at the other drifting end could not help him; it was more than enough for them to look after themselves. For the White Whale's aspect as he revolved was so appalling, and the ever-tightening circles he made were so swift, like a planet's, that he seemed to be swooping horizontally upon them. And though the other boats, unharmed, still hovered close by, they dared not pull into the eddy to strike, for fear that would be the signal for the instant destruction of the endangered castaways, Ahab and all; nor in that case could they themselves hope to escape. So, with straining eyes, they stayed on the outer edge of the dreadful zone, whose center had now become the old man's head.

Meanwhile, from the beginning all this had been seen from the ship's mastheads; and squaring her yards, she had borne down upon the scene; and was now so near that Ahab in the water hailed her! "Sail on the" — but that moment a breaking sea dashed on him from Moby Dick, and overwhelmed him for the time. But struggling out of it again, and chancing to rise on a towering crest, he shouted: "Sail on the whale! Drive him off!"
The Pequod's bows were pointed at them; breaking up the charmed circle, she succeeded in separating the white whale from his victim. As he swam sullenly away, the boats flew to the rescue.

Ahab was dragged into Stubb's boat with bloodshot, blinded eyes, the white brine caking in his wrinkles; and the long tension of his bodily strength cracked, and helplessly he yielded to his body's doom: for a time, lying all crushed in the bottom of Stubb's boat, like one trodden underfoot by herds of elephants. Far inland, nameless wails came from him, like desolate sounds from out of ravines.

But the very intensity of his physical collapse only made it the shorter. Within the span of an instant, great hearts sometimes condense into one deep pang the sum total of those shallow pains that are mercifully spread through the whole lives of feebler men. And so such hearts, though brief in each single suffering, still, if the gods decree it, pile up in their lifetime a whole age of woe, made up entirely of instantaneous intensities; for even in their centers, mere points though these are, those noble natures contain the entire circumferences of inferior souls.
"The harpoon," said Ahab, half-rising and draggingly leaning on one bent arm — "is it safe?"
"Aye, sir, for it was not darted; this is it," said Stubb, showing it.
"Lay it before me; any missing men?"
"One, two, three, four, five; there were five oars, sir, and here are five men."

"That's good. Help me, man; I wish to stand. So, so, I see him! There! There! Going to leeward still; what a leaping spout! — Hands off from me! The eternal sap runs up in Ahab's bones again! Set the sail; out oars; the helm!"

It often happens that when a boat is stove, its crew, once picked up by another boat, help to work that second boat; and the chase is then continued with what are called double-banked oars. So it was now. But the added power of the boat did not match the added power of the whale, for he seemed to have treble-banked every fin, swimming at a speed that plainly showed that if the chase were pushed on now, under these circumstances, it would prove an indefinitely prolonged one, if not a hopeless one; nor could any crew endure such unbroken, intense straining at the oar for so long a period — a thing barely bearable even for one brief spell. The ship itself, then, as sometimes happens, offered the most promising way of overtaking the chase in the meantime. Accordingly, the boats now made for her and were soon swayed up to their cranes — the two parts of the wrecked boat having already been secured by her — and then, hoisting everything up to her side, piling her canvas high, and stretching it out sideways with stunsails like the double-jointed wings of an albatross, the Pequod bore down in Moby Dick's leeward wake. At the familiar, regular intervals, the whale's glittering spout was duly announced from the manned mastheads; and whenever he was reported as just gone down, Ahab would note the time, and then, pacing the deck binnacle-watch in hand, the moment the last second of the allotted hour ran out, his voice was heard: "Whose is the doubloon now? Do you see him?" And if the reply was "No, sir!" he at once ordered them to hoist him to his perch. In this way the day wore on; Ahab now aloft and motionless, now pacing the planks without rest.

As he walked like this, making no sound except to hail the men aloft or to tell them to hoist a sail still higher or spread one still wider — pacing back and forth like this beneath his slouched hat — at every turn he passed his own wrecked boat, which had been dropped onto the quarter-deck and lay there upside down, broken bow to shattered stern. At last he stopped in front of it; and just as fresh troops of clouds will sometimes sail across a sky that is already overcast, so some such added gloom now crept over the old man's face.

Stubb saw him stop; and perhaps meaning — though not vainly — to show that his own courage was undiminished, and so keep a brave place in his Captain's thoughts, he stepped forward and, eyeing the wreck, exclaimed, "The thistle the ass refused; it pricked his mouth too sharply, sir; ha! ha!"

"What soulless thing is this that laughs in front of a wreck? Man, man! If I did not know you to be as brave as fearless fire (and as mechanical), I could swear you were a coward. Neither groan nor laugh should be heard in front of a wreck."
"Aye, sir," said Starbuck, drawing near, "it is a solemn sight; an omen, and an ill one."

"Omen? Omen? — the dictionary! If the gods mean to speak outright to man, they will honorably speak outright; not shake their heads and give an old wives' dark hint. — Begone! You two are the opposite poles of one thing; Starbuck is Stubb reversed, and Stubb is Starbuck; and you two are all mankind; and Ahab stands alone among the millions of the peopled earth, with neither gods nor men for his neighbors! Cold, cold — I shiver! — What now? Aloft there! Do you see him? Sing out for every spout, even if he spouts ten times a second!"
The day was nearly done; only the hem of its golden robe was rustling. Soon it was almost dark, but the lookout men still remained at their posts.
"Can't see the spout now, sir; too dark," cried a voice from the air.
"How heading when last seen?"
"As before, sir — straight to leeward."

"Good! He will travel slower now that it's night. Down royals and topgallant stunsails, Mr. Starbuck. We must not run over him before morning; he's making a passage now, and may heave to for a while. Helm there! Keep her full before the wind! — Aloft! Come down! — Mr. Stubb, send a fresh hand to the fore-masthead, and see that it's manned till morning." Then, advancing toward the doubloon on the mainmast: "Men, this gold is mine, for I earned it; but I shall let it stay here till the White Whale is dead; and then, whichever of you first raises him on the day he is killed, this gold is that man's; and if on that day I raise him again myself, then ten times its sum shall be divided among all of you! Away now! — the deck is yours, sir!"
Saying this, he stationed himself halfway inside the scuttle, pulled his hat down low, and stood there until dawn, except when he roused himself now and then to see how the night was going.
